name: Sport-related concussion
summary: A traumatic brain injury from a blow or impulsive force to the head, causing short-lived neurological impairment. Check red flags first. Imaging is normally normal, and most people recover within weeks.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Mean 14.0 days to symptom-free (95% CI 12.7–15.4) in a meta-analysis of 278 studies, with very high heterogeneity; most people recover within weeks

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Staged and criteria-based. Mean 19.8 days to return to sport, about twice the 8.3 days to return to school

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Diagnosis is clinical. The SCAT6 is most useful within 72 hours of injury and loses utility by 7 days

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Normally normal. CT is used only to exclude intracranial injury when red flags or a decision rule call for it

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Pooled youth incidence 1.41 per 1000 athlete exposures across 21 sports; highest in taekwondo, rugby union and ice hockey

overview:
Red flags come first. Any deteriorating consciousness, worsening or severe headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, focal neurological sign, neck pain or tenderness, anticoagulant use, intoxication, or sign of skull fracture or cerebrospinal fluid leak means the athlete is not managed as a simple concussion. Remove them from play and arrange emergency assessment [r1,r2,r3].

Sport-related concussion (SRC) is a traumatic brain injury caused by a direct blow to the head, or by a blow to the face, neck or body that transmits an impulsive force to the head. It produces a rapid-onset, short-lived impairment of neurological function that resolves spontaneously in most people, reflects a functional disturbance rather than a structural injury, and shows no abnormality on standard CT or MRI [r4,r5]. The diagnosis is therefore clinical. The brain's response is described as a neurometabolic cascade of ionic flux, glutamate release and an energy mismatch [r6].

Most people recover within weeks. In a meta-analysis of 278 studies, the mean time to symptom-free was 14.0 days and the mean time to return to sport was 19.8 days, although the studies were very heterogeneous and only 7.9% were rated high quality [r7]. A minority have persisting symptoms, which is the subject of a separate page. Management is built on early recognition, removal from play, brief relative rest, early symptom-limited activity, graded return to learn and a staged return to sport [r5,r8,r9].

epidemiology.text: In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 116 prospective studies of children and adolescents (about 3 million participants), the pooled concussion incidence was 1.41 per 1000 athlete exposures across 21 sports and 4.36 per 1000 player hours across 7 sports. The highest rates per 1000 athlete exposures were in taekwondo, rugby union and ice hockey, and the highest per 1000 player hours were in rugby sevens, rugby league and rugby union [r10]. Recovery varies. In a meta-analysis of 278 studies, point estimates suggested that female athletes and younger cohorts might take longer to recover, but confidence intervals overlapped, so the authors judged that recovery patterns are broadly similar across sex and age [r7]. In a prospective cohort of 3063 children and adolescents seen in emergency departments, 31.0% of the 2584 who completed follow-up had persistent post-concussion symptoms at 28 days [r11].

intrinsic: Factors linked to slower recovery rather than to injury itself: a higher initial symptom burden was the strongest predictor of a longer time to return to sport [r7]
Migraine history and premorbid or postmorbid depression and anxiety may modify recovery time [r7]

In children and adolescents, risk of persistent symptoms rose with female sex, age 13 or older, a physician-diagnosed migraine history and a previous concussion with symptoms lasting more than a week [r11]
Neck strength and tackle technique are proposed modifiable factors, but the systematic review judged that more research was needed [r12]
extrinsic: Contact and collision sports: incidence is highest in taekwondo, rugby union and ice hockey in youth athletes [r10]

Rules that allow high-contact play. A policy disallowing body checking in child and adolescent ice hockey was associated with a 58% lower concussion rate (IRR 0.42, 95% CI 0.33–0.53), and limiting contact in American football practice with a 64% lower practice concussion rate [r12]
No mouthguard in collision sport: mouthguards were protective (IRR 0.74, 95% CI 0.64–0.89) [r12]
Continuing to play after the injury and delayed access to a health professional were associated with longer recovery (modifiable by sideline recognition and removal from play) [r7]

mechanism.summary: Concussion follows a direct blow to the head, or an impulsive force transmitted to the head from a blow to the face, neck or body [r4,r5]. The head accelerates both linearly and in rotation. The brain floats in cerebrospinal fluid, so it lags the skull, strikes the inner table under the impact (coup), then rebounds against the opposite pole (contrecoup). Rotational acceleration also strains the white matter [r13]. The common trigger is a head-to-head, head-to-shoulder or head-to-ground collision.
sequence: Two players collide at speed, or an athlete falls, and the head is struck or abruptly stopped.
An impulsive force is transmitted to the head, which accelerates linearly and rotates around the neck [r14].
The skull stops or is driven backwards, but the brain, floating in cerebrospinal fluid, lags and then strikes the skull under the point of impact (coup).
The brain rebounds and strikes the opposite pole (contrecoup). Rotation strains the white matter, including the brainstem [r13].
Axons and cell membranes are stretched, and ions flow across the membranes with release of glutamate [r6].
The injured brain meets a high energy demand in a period of metabolic crisis, which produces headache, dizziness, fogginess, slowed thinking and balance impairment [r6].
Consciousness may be lost briefly in a minority, but most concussions occur without loss of consciousness, and the athlete may continue playing unless the injury is recognised.

variants.name: Direct blow to the head
variants.description: Head-to-head, head-to-shoulder or head-to-ground contact. The force is delivered at the point of impact, with the coup and contrecoup motion of the brain.

variants.name: Impulsive force from the body
variants.description: A blow to the chest, trunk or neck, or sudden deceleration, can transmit an impulsive force to the head without any head contact [r4,r5].

variants.name: Rotational acceleration
variants.description: In a swine model scaled from human concussion thresholds, head rotation caused widespread axonal pathology. Rotation in the axial plane (transverse to the brainstem) produced more brainstem pathology and a 10–35 minute loss of consciousness, whereas coronal rotation did not [r13].

variants.name: Repetitive head impacts
variants.description: Repeated sub-concussive impacts occur in collision sports. A systematic review of case-control and cohort studies found no increased risk of mental health or neurological disease in former amateur athletes, with some signals in former professionals that need higher-quality confirmation [r15].

anatomy.text: The brain sits inside the skull, cushioned by a thin layer of cerebrospinal fluid and held by the meninges. The cerebral hemispheres are joined by the corpus callosum, and the brainstem passes through the foramen magnum to the upper cervical spine. The head rests on the cervical spine, whose muscles and joints control head motion, so a head impact is also a neck loading event. The vestibular labyrinth and the oculomotor system share central pathways with the brain and are frequently affected [r16].

structures.name: Cerebral cortex and subcortical white matter
structures.role: Cognition, attention and memory. Axons here are stretched during rotational acceleration [r13]

structures.name: Corpus callosum
structures.role: Interhemispheric white matter tract. A central, midline structure in sagittal section where rotational strain concentrates

structures.name: Brainstem
structures.role: Consciousness, autonomic and oculomotor control. Axial rotation produced more brainstem axonal pathology in a swine model [r13]

structures.name: Cerebellum
structures.role: Balance, coordination and oculomotor control, below the tentorium

structures.name: Cerebrospinal fluid space and skull
structures.role: Cushion between brain and skull. The brain moves within it, so the coup and contrecoup contacts occur at the poles

structures.name: Blood-brain barrier
structures.role: Regulates entry of serum proteins. Disrupted at tissue interfaces after rotational injury in swine [r17]

structures.name: Upper cervical spine and neck muscles
structures.role: Carry the head, are loaded in the same event, and can generate headache and dizziness after concussion [r18]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Concussion produces a functional disturbance of the brain that results from a cascade of ionic, metabolic and physiological events. The initial ionic flux and glutamate release create a high energy demand and a period of metabolic crisis in the injured brain. These perturbations can be linked to migrainous symptoms, vulnerability to repeat injury and cognitive impairment [r6]. Standard CT and MRI are normally normal, because the injury is chiefly functional [r4].

Animal work shows that the injury is not trivial at the microscopic level. In a swine model of head rotational acceleration scaled from human concussion thresholds, extensive axonal pathology appeared throughout the white matter by 7 days, even without a sustained loss of consciousness [r13]. In a related model, serum proteins crossed the blood-brain barrier at 6–72 hours at gray-white boundaries, periventricular and subpial regions, without haemorrhage [r17]. These are animal findings and have not been shown to match the clinical course in athletes.

structures.name: White matter axons
structures.effect: Stretched by rotational acceleration, with swollen axonal bulbs in swine [r13]

structures.name: Cortex under the impact and at the opposite pole
structures.effect: Coup and contrecoup contact between brain and skull; a contusion on CT would be a more serious injury than concussion

structures.name: Brainstem
structures.effect: More axonal pathology with axial-plane rotation in swine, which may relate to loss of consciousness [r13]

structures.name: Blood-brain barrier
structures.effect: Multifocal, transient disruption after experimental concussion, at interfaces between tissues of different material properties [r17]

structures.name: Cervical spine
structures.effect: May be injured in the same event. Dizziness, neck pain and headache can have a cervical source [r18]

muscles.name: Neck muscles
muscles.effect: Protective guarding and neck pain after the impact, which contributes to headache and dizziness. Cervical physiotherapy was part of the intervention that shortened time to clearance in the persistent-symptom trial [r18]

muscles.name: Oculomotor muscles and control
muscles.effect: Oculomotor, cervical and vestibular impairments were assessed in 76 studies in the acute-evaluation review, which supports screening of these systems in every athlete [r16]

muscles.name: General deconditioning
muscles.effect: Strict rest for 5 days gave no benefit and was followed by more daily symptoms than usual care, so prolonged inactivity is not protective [r8]

cellular.description: Stretch of axons and membranes allows ionic flux and release of glutamate, the start of the neurometabolic cascade [r6].
The ionic flux creates a high energy demand and a period of metabolic crisis in the injured brain [r6].

cellular.timing: 6–72 hours and about 7 days in swine
cellular.description: Blood-brain barrier disruption was seen at 6–72 hours and axonal pathology at 7 days in swine models [r17,r13].
Mean time to symptom-free was 14.0 days in a meta-analysis, with wide variation. Biological recovery has not been shown to track symptom resolution in the sources reviewed [r7].

systems.effect: Early exercise intolerance after concussion: a lower heart-rate threshold at symptom exacerbation on the Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test on visit 1 was strongly associated with prolonged recovery [r19].
Each can contribute to dizziness, headache and visual symptoms. Cervicovestibular rehabilitation shortened time to clearance in people with persistent symptoms [r18,r20].
Premorbid and postmorbid depression and anxiety, and migraine history, may modify recovery time, so mood and sleep belong in every assessment [r7].
Most athletes had a full return to learn by 10 days without new academic support, but those who struggle need adjustments [r7].
Transient blood-brain barrier disruption was found at 6–72 hours in swine [r17]. The clinical significance in people is not established in the sources reviewed.

timeframes.summary: Most athletes recover within weeks. A meta-analysis of 278 studies found a mean of 14.0 days to symptom-free, 8.3 days to return to learn and 19.8 days to return to sport, with high heterogeneity [r7]. Time points are averages, not rules: return to sport is decided by criteria.

healing.description: Ionic flux, glutamate release and energy mismatch; timing in people varies (illustrative range) [r6]

healing.phase: Symptom-limited rest and early light activity
healing.description: Brief relative rest, then gradual return to normal activity; subsymptom aerobic exercise started within 10 days speeds recovery in adolescents [r21,r9]
Mean 14.0 days to symptom-free, with wide variation; most are recovered within weeks [r7]

healing.phase: Return to learn then graded return to sport
healing.description: Mean 8.3 days to return to learn and 19.8 days to return to sport [r7]
Symptoms beyond the expected window; persistent post-concussion symptoms at 28 days occurred in 30–31% of children and adolescents in two cohorts [r11,r22]

milestones.label: SCAT6 most useful
milestones.note: Maximal utility in the first 72 hours, diminishing up to 7 days [r16]

milestones.label: Full return to learn (93%)
milestones.note: 93% of athletes had a full return to learn by 10 days without new academic support [r7]

milestones.label: Mean return to sport
milestones.note: Mean 19.8 days (95% CI 18.8–20.7), after a staged protocol [r7]

milestones.label: 28-day persisting-symptom threshold
milestones.note: 30.4% of 2413 children had persistent post-concussion symptoms at 28 days [r22]

timeframes.returnToSport: Staged and criteria-based, never time-based or same-day. In a meta-analysis the mean time to return to sport was 19.8 days, with high heterogeneity, after a return to learn [r7]. Athletes with a higher initial symptom burden take longer [r7].

symptoms: Headache or a feeling of pressure in the head, often the most frequent symptom
Dizziness, balance problems and feeling off balance
Nausea, with or without vomiting (repeated vomiting is a red flag)
Mental fogginess, slowed thinking, difficulty concentrating or remembering
Sensitivity to light or noise, blurred vision, and tiredness
Emotional change: irritability, sadness or anxiety, and sleep disturbance
signs: Observed loss of consciousness, a slow getting-up, a vacant look, or a lying motionless on the ground (loss of consciousness is not required for the diagnosis)
Impaired balance or gait, such as an unsteady stance or stumbling
Slowed responses, confusion, disorientation, or memory loss for the event
Oculomotor or vestibular signs on screening, such as symptom provocation with eye tracking or head movement [r16]
Neck tenderness or restricted cervical movement, which may mean a coexisting neck injury [r18]

subjective: Mechanism: direct blow, collision, fall or impulsive force; the height or speed; whether helmeted; whether there was an obvious impact to the head, face or neck
Immediate features: loss of consciousness, amnesia for the event, a witness account, and whether the athlete kept playing (continued play is linked to longer recovery) [r7]
Current symptoms using a graded symptom scale, with time of onset and trend (rising symptoms or delayed onset need urgent review)
Red-flag screen first: worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, limb weakness, neck pain, drug or alcohol use, anticoagulants
History of previous concussions and how long they lasted, migraine, learning difficulty, depression or anxiety, and sleep problems [r11,r7]
Home and school or work circumstances, and demands such as exams, which guide return-to-learn advice
observation: Level of alertness and response to commands, speech, and orientation
Gait, posture and balance on standing and tandem walk
Facial or scalp injuries, haematoma, bruising behind the ear or around the eyes, and any fluid from the ear or nose
Pupil size and reactions; eye movements for smooth pursuit and saccades
palpation: Cervical spine: midline and paraspinal tenderness, suboccipital muscle tone and upper cervical segment tenderness
Scalp and facial bones: depression, step or swelling that could indicate a fracture
rangeOfMotion: Active cervical range in all planes; pain or restriction can mean cervical injury, which is assessed only after a cervical spine injury has been excluded [r18]
Provocation of dizziness or headache with end-range cervical movement
strength: Screen upper and lower limb power for focal weakness (a red flag)
Deep neck flexor and neck extensor endurance in persisting symptoms or neck pain, not in the acute setting
neuro: Cranial nerves, including pupils and eye movements, and facial symmetry
Limb power, sensation, reflexes and coordination (finger-nose, heel-shin) for focal deficit
Cognitive screen: orientation, immediate and delayed recall, and concentration (the SCAT6 uses a 10-word list because the 5-word list showed a ceiling effect) [r16]
Balance testing (modified Balance Error Scoring System) and tandem gait [r11]
Vestibular and oculomotor screen: smooth pursuit, saccades, near point of convergence, vestibulo-ocular reflex and visual motion sensitivity [r16]
functional: Exercise tolerance with the Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test when the athlete is safe to exercise: the heart rate at symptom exacerbation guides prescription and prognosis [r19]
Return-to-learn tolerance: ability to read, use screens and sit through a class without symptom rise
Sport-specific tasks only after symptom-free at rest and on graded exercise

specialTests.name: Sport Concussion Assessment Tool 6 (SCAT6) and Child SCAT6
specialTests.purpose: Structured acute assessment: symptom score, cognitive screen, neurological examination, balance and delayed recall
specialTests.procedure: Complete the red-flag screen and sideline check, then the symptom checklist, orientation and memory (10-word list), concentration, neck and neurological examination, balance (mBESS) and delayed recall. Compare with the athlete's baseline or normative values.
specialTests.positive: New symptoms or a deficit relative to baseline or norms, interpreted together with the clinical picture. The SCAT discriminated concussed from non-concussed athletes within 72 hours, with diminishing utility up to 7 days and limited utility as a return-to-play tool beyond 7 days. Accuracy figures were not extracted for this page.

specialTests.name: Vestibular and Ocular Motor Screening (VOMS) and eye-movement testing
specialTests.purpose: Screen the vestibular and oculomotor systems, which are often impaired and can persist
specialTests.procedure: Test smooth pursuit, horizontal and vertical saccades, near point of convergence, horizontal vestibulo-ocular reflex and visual motion sensitivity. Rate any provocation of headache, dizziness, nausea or fogginess.
specialTests.positive: Provocation of symptoms or an abnormal near point of convergence. Scoring conventions and cut-offs vary and were not verified here; use clinical judgement and re-test over time.

specialTests.name: Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test (BCTT)
specialTests.purpose: Measure exercise tolerance, set a safe heart-rate threshold for exercise prescription and inform prognosis
specialTests.procedure: A graded treadmill walk with a stepped increase in incline at a fixed speed, recording heart rate and symptom rating each minute; the test stops when symptoms increase or the athlete reaches maximal exertion. The heart rate at stopping is the threshold.
specialTests.positive: Symptom exacerbation at a low heart rate. A lower heart-rate threshold on day 1 was strongly associated with a longer recovery. Doing the test within a week did not delay recovery or raise symptoms the next day.

specialTests.name: Tandem stance error count (Balance Error Scoring System)
specialTests.purpose: Measure postural stability and add prognostic information in children and adolescents
specialTests.procedure: The athlete stands heel-to-toe on a firm surface with eyes closed for 20 seconds; count the errors (opening the eyes, stepping, falling, lifting a hand off the hips).
specialTests.positive: Four or more errors in tandem stance was one of nine variables in the paediatric risk score for persistent symptoms. The whole score had only modest discrimination (AUC 0.68–0.71).

specialTests.name: Cervical spine examination
specialTests.purpose: Exclude a cervical injury first, then identify a cervical contribution to headache and dizziness
specialTests.procedure: If there is any neck pain, tenderness or neurological symptom, keep the spine immobilised and arrange emergency assessment. Otherwise assess active range, segmental tenderness and movement-provoked dizziness or headache.
specialTests.positive: Neck pain, restricted range or provoked dizziness or headache. Cervical and vestibular physiotherapy shortened time to clearance in people with persistent symptoms.

clinicalRules.name: PECARN head-injury rules (children)
clinicalRules.description: For children aged 2 years and older, the very-low-risk criteria are normal mental status, no loss of consciousness, no vomiting, a non-severe injury mechanism, no signs of basilar skull fracture and no severe headache. The rule had a negative predictive value of 99.95% (3798/3800) and a sensitivity of 96.8% (61/63) for clinically important brain injury, so CT is unnecessary in this group. Under 2 years, the criteria are normal mental status, no scalp haematoma except frontal, no loss of consciousness or less than 5 seconds, a non-severe mechanism, no palpable skull fracture and acting normally per the parents [r1].

clinicalRules.name: CDC paediatric mild TBI guideline
clinicalRules.description: 19 sets of recommendations on diagnosis, prognosis and management, covering imaging, symptom scales, cognitive testing, counselling, rest, return to school and symptom management [r2].

clinicalRules.name: Adult outpatient TBI guideline
clinicalRules.description: Recommendations include confirming the diagnosis, determining whether emergency department evaluation is required, requesting imaging and neuropsychological assessment when indicated, assessing the risk of persistent symptoms and guiding return to usual activities [r3].

outcomeMeasures.name: Graded symptom scale (SCAT6 symptom score; Post-Concussion Symptom Inventory)
outcomeMeasures.use: Track symptom burden. Three or more new or worsening symptoms at 28 days defined persistent post-concussion symptoms in the paediatric cohorts [r11,r22].

outcomeMeasures.name: Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test heart-rate threshold
outcomeMeasures.use: Exercise tolerance and recovery marker; normalisation of exercise tolerance was part of the recovery definition in the aerobic exercise trials [r21,r19]

outcomeMeasures.name: Days to symptom-free, return to learn and return to sport
outcomeMeasures.use: Record each milestone. The reference means were 14.0, 8.3 and 19.8 days [r7].

outcomeMeasures.name: Paediatric persistent-symptom risk score (5P)
outcomeMeasures.use: A 12-point score using sex, age, migraine history, prior concussion, headache, noise sensitivity, fatigue, slowed answers and tandem-stance errors. Discrimination was modest (AUC 0.68–0.71), so use it to prompt closer follow-up, not to decide care [r11].

imaging.indication: Red flags, a failed clinical decision rule, anticoagulation, a high-risk mechanism or deterioration; follow the PECARN criteria in children and the local adult rule
imaging.findings: Normal in concussion. Used to exclude fracture and intracranial haemorrhage [r1,r3].

imaging.indication: Not routine. Consider for persisting or atypical symptoms, new focal signs or when another diagnosis is suspected
imaging.findings: Usually normal. Research techniques are not part of routine diagnosis [r4].

imaging.indication: Neck pain, tenderness, neurological symptoms or a high-risk mechanism; follow the local cervical spine rule
imaging.findings: Excludes fracture or instability before any neck movement is tested

differentials.name: Intracranial haemorrhage or skull fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Deteriorating consciousness, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, focal signs, or signs of basilar skull fracture; CT shows the lesion. This is an emergency [r1].

differentials.name: Cervical spine fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Midline neck pain or tenderness, limb neurological symptoms or a high-energy mechanism; immobilise and image before any neck movement.

differentials.name: Whiplash-associated disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Neck pain and stiffness are the main problem after an acceleration-deceleration injury, with less cognitive and balance involvement; can coexist with concussion.

differentials.name: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
differentials.distinguishing: Brief spinning vertigo provoked by head position change and a positive Dix-Hallpike test; can follow head trauma.

differentials.name: Cervicogenic headache and cervicogenic dizziness
differentials.distinguishing: Dizziness or headache linked to neck movement or posture, with neck findings; a diagnosis of exclusion.

differentials.name: Persisting post-concussion symptoms
differentials.distinguishing: Symptoms that go beyond the expected recovery window; use the persisting-symptoms pathway rather than repeated acute concussion advice.

differentials.name: Migraine, dehydration, hypoglycaemia, exertional heat illness, cardiac or substance-related causes
differentials.distinguishing: Symptoms can mimic concussion on the sideline; check observations, glucose, temperature and substance use, and do not diagnose concussion in an intoxicated athlete.

redFlags: Deteriorating level of consciousness, increasing drowsiness, or loss of consciousness with deterioration, confusion that worsens, or a GCS fall: this is an emergency. Call an ambulance, protect the airway, keep the neck still and do not leave the athlete alone [r1,r2].
Worsening or severe headache, or repeated vomiting: arrange emergency department assessment and CT the same day. Both are components of the PECARN rule for children aged 2 years and older [r1].
Seizure, or a focal neurological sign (unequal pupils, limb weakness or numbness, facial droop, speech disturbance, double vision, loss of coordination): emergency transfer.

Neck pain or tenderness, or neurological symptoms in the limbs after the impact: suspect cervical spine injury. Immobilise the spine, do not remove a helmet unless trained, and arrange emergency assessment.

Signs of skull fracture or CSF leak (clear fluid from the nose or ear, bruising behind the ear or around the eyes, blood behind the eardrum, palpable skull depression): emergency department assessment [r1].
Anticoagulant, antiplatelet or bleeding-disorder use, older age, or a high-energy mechanism (fall from height, vehicle, bicycle): CT and medical review, even if symptoms are mild [r3].
Intoxication with alcohol or drugs, which confounds assessment: do not diagnose or clear the athlete. Arrange observation with a responsible adult and review when sober.
Symptoms that worsen over hours to days, new neurological signs on re-check, or persisting symptoms with a red flag at any time: urgent medical review.

management.principles: Management has four parts. First, recognise the injury and remove the athlete from play: continuing to play and delayed access to care were associated with longer recovery [r7]. Second, screen for red flags and arrange emergency care when any is present [r1,r2]. Third, give brief relative rest, then encourage early symptom-limited activity, because strict rest for 5 days gave no added benefit and more daily symptoms [r8], while early subsymptom aerobic exercise sped recovery in adolescents [r21,r9]. Fourth, plan a staged return to learn and then a staged return to sport [r5]. The athlete decides the pace together with the clinician, and symptoms guide progression. For adolescents and adults with dizziness, neck pain or headaches beyond 10 days, individualised cervicovestibular rehabilitation is recommended [r20].

medical.name: Emergency assessment, CT and observation when red flags or a decision rule apply
medical.description: A doctor reviews the athlete, orders CT where indicated and arranges observation. Decision rules identify patients at very low risk for whom CT is unnecessary; for example the PECARN rule for age 2 years and older had a negative predictive value of 99.95% [r1]. Guidelines address imaging in children and adults [r2,r3].

medical.name: Simple analgesia for headache
medical.description: Paracetamol for headache after the red flags are excluded. Avoid masking symptoms that guide return to sport decisions. No drug was shown to speed recovery in the sources reviewed.

medical.name: Specialist and neuropsychological referral when recovery is slow or atypical
medical.description: Refer to a sports or rehabilitation physician, neurologist or neuropsychologist when symptoms persist, recovery is atypical or return-to-learn is difficult. Guidelines list neuropsychological assessment when indicated and deciding if and when to refer to specialty care [r3].

physio.name: Immediate removal from play and no same-day return
physio.description: Any athlete with suspected concussion is removed from play and not allowed to return that day. Continuing to play was associated with longer recovery in a meta-analysis [r7].

physio.name: Brief relative rest then early symptom-limited activity
physio.description: Rest for the first 24–48 hours (clinical convention), then return to daily activity and light movement within symptom tolerance. Adolescents told to rest strictly for 5 days did no better, and reported more daily symptoms (total score 187.9 versus 131.9) than those given usual care [r8]. In a large cohort, physical activity within 7 days was associated with a lower risk of persistent symptoms at 28 days (24.6% versus 43.5% unadjusted; RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65–0.84 after weighting), although this was observational [r22].

physio.name: Subsymptom-threshold aerobic exercise (adolescents, within 10 days)
physio.description: Individualised aerobic exercise about 20 minutes a day below the symptom threshold, with the threshold set by treadmill test. In 103 adolescents, median recovery was 13 versus 17 days with stretching (P = .009) [r21]. In a replication of 118 adolescents, those on aerobic exercise were more likely to recover within 4 weeks, with a 48% reduced risk of persistent symptoms (hazard ratio for stretching versus aerobic 0.52, 95% CI 0.28–0.97) and no adverse events [r9]. Both trials are from one research group in adolescents only.

physio.name: Graded return to learn
physio.description: Students return to school with adjustments tied to symptoms. In a meta-analysis, 93% of athletes had a full return to learn by 10 days without new academic support, so plan extra supports for the few who struggle [r7].

physio.name: Cervicovestibular rehabilitation for dizziness, neck pain or headaches beyond 10 days
physio.description: Combined cervical spine physiotherapy and vestibular rehabilitation. In a randomised trial of 31 people, 73% (11/15) were medically cleared within 8 weeks versus 7% (1/14) of controls (HR 3.91, 95% CI 1.34–11.34) [r18]. The systematic review recommends it for adolescents and adults with dizziness, neck pain or headaches beyond 10 days [r20].

physio.name: Staged return-to-sport protocol
physio.description: A stepwise progression from symptom-limited activity through aerobic, sport-specific, non-contact and full-contact training to match play, with progression only when symptom-free at each step. The consensus statements endorse graded return to sport [r5,r4].

physio.name: Strict rest for several days
physio.description: Five days of strict rest gave no added benefit over usual care and was followed by more daily symptoms [r8].

physio.name: Using the SCAT6 alone to clear an athlete beyond the first week
physio.description: The SCAT has limited utility as a return-to-play tool beyond 7 days after injury, so clearance needs a full clinical assessment and a staged return [r16].

education: Most people recover within a few weeks. Expect some days of symptoms and gradual improvement.
Rest only for the first day or two, then return to normal activity at a level that does not make symptoms much worse.
Do not return to sport the same day, and do not return to contact sport until you have no symptoms, are back at school or work, and have completed the staged return.
Seek urgent medical help if headache worsens, vomiting continues, you become very drowsy or confused, you have a seizure, weakness, or neck pain.
Avoid alcohol and other drugs while recovering.
Tell the school or workplace. Most students are back in class within 10 days, and adjustments are available if you struggle.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based. Symptoms guide each step: move on only when the athlete has been symptom-free (or within an agreed mild, brief symptom rise) at the current level. Stage durations are typical, and an athlete may spend days or weeks at one stage. After a short period of relative rest, aerobic activity below the symptom threshold is prescribed, ideally based on a treadmill test [r9,r19]. Return to learn runs alongside the stages and comes before return to sport [r7,r5]. Dosages are typical clinical ranges, with the 20-minute aerobic dose taken from the trials [r21,r9]. An athlete who plateaus or has dizziness, neck pain or headaches beyond 10 days is referred for cervicovestibular assessment [r20].

stages.name: Relative rest and education
goals: Remove from play and exclude red flags
Explain the expected course and what to do
Allow symptoms to settle, then start gentle daily activity
precautions: No driving or work at height until symptoms settle (clinical convention)
Strict rest for days is not advised [r8]
Re-check for red flags if symptoms worsen

exercises.name: Easy walking around the house or short outdoor walks
exercises.dosage: 5–15 minutes, several times a day, symptoms staying mild
exercises.cues: Keep the pace comfortable. Stop if headache or dizziness clearly worsens.

exercises.name: Light daily tasks and short screen or reading blocks
exercises.dosage: 10–20 minutes, then a break, repeated through the day
exercises.cues: Build up gradually; symptoms may rise briefly but should settle

exercises.name: Sleep routine and hydration
exercises.dosage: Regular sleep and wake times; no alcohol

exercises.name: Gentle neck range of motion if no neck injury is suspected
exercises.dosage: 5 slow turns each way, 2–3 times a day
exercises.cues: Stop for any neck pain, arm symptoms or dizziness; only after a cervical injury is excluded

progressionCriteria: Symptoms stable or improving, with no red flags
Able to walk 10–15 minutes without symptom increase

stages.name: Subsymptom aerobic exercise and return to learn
goals: Raise heart rate safely below the symptom threshold
precautions: Keep heart rate below the symptom-exacerbation threshold (a common clinical convention is about 80% of the treadmill test threshold)
Stop if symptoms rise clearly above the resting level
No contact, no heading, no risk of head impact

exercises.name: Stationary cycle or treadmill walk at 80% of the threshold heart rate
exercises.dosage: 20 minutes a day (the daily dose in the exercise trials [r21,r9]), repeated daily and increased in effort as the threshold rises
exercises.cues: Heart-rate monitor on; symptoms should stay at or near the resting level

exercises.name: Symptom-guided school or work re-entry
exercises.dosage: Half days, then full days, with breaks and agreed adjustments
exercises.cues: Aim for a full return to learn within about 10 days; most athletes manage this without extra support [r7]

exercises.name: Light mobility and stretching, as a control for non-aerobic exercise
exercises.cues: Easy movement only, not a substitute for aerobic work [r21]

progressionCriteria: Tolerates 20 minutes of aerobic exercise without symptom increase
Back at school or work at normal hours, or near it
Treadmill-test threshold rising, or symptoms at rest minimal

stages.name: Sport-specific exercise and balance
goals: Add sport-specific movement without head-impact risk
precautions: Symptoms stay at or below the resting level
Stop and re-assess if dizziness or headache returns

exercises.name: Running at progressively higher intensity
exercises.dosage: 20–30 minutes, building from 60% to 80% of maximal effort over several sessions (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Smooth running, no jumping or heading

exercises.name: Single-leg balance, then with head turns
exercises.dosage: 3 × 30 seconds each leg, eyes open then closed, daily
exercises.cues: Stand near a wall for safety; stop if dizzy

exercises.name: Gaze stabilisation (vestibulo-ocular reflex) exercise
exercises.dosage: Fix gaze on a target while turning the head side to side, 3 × 30 seconds, daily
exercises.cues: Mild dizziness is acceptable if it settles within minutes; stop if it lingers

exercises.name: Deep neck flexor activation (chin nod)
exercises.cues: Gentle nod, not a chin poke; hold with normal breathing

exercises.name: Sport-specific drills without contact
exercises.dosage: Ball skills, running and passing for 20–30 minutes, 3–4 times a week

progressionCriteria: Symptom-free at rest and with sport-specific exercise
Balance and vestibular-oculomotor screens normal or near normal
No symptom flare in the 24 hours after training (clinical convention)

stages.name: Non-contact training and resistance work
goals: Add complex, high-intensity drills and resistance training
Restore sport-specific coordination, speed and decision making
precautions: Return to full school or work first
Stop and step back if symptoms return
At least 24 hours between steps (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Higher-intensity running and sprint drills
exercises.dosage: 3–4 sessions a week, progressing speed and direction changes
exercises.cues: Smooth change of direction; monitor for headache or dizziness

exercises.name: Resistance training (squat, hinge, push, pull)
exercises.cues: Avoid breath-holding and heavy Valsalva efforts early on

exercises.name: Neck isometric strengthening
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10-second holds in four directions, 3 times a week
exercises.cues: Light to moderate effort, no pain or dizziness

exercises.name: Sport-specific drills with decision making
exercises.dosage: Passing, dodging and agility drills in a team setting without contact, 3–4 times a week

progressionCriteria: Symptom-free during and after training for at least 24 hours

stages.name: Full-contact practice and return to sport
goals: Return to full-contact training, then match play
Confirm the athlete can tolerate collisions without symptoms
Agree a monitoring plan with coach and athlete
precautions: Step back one stage for any symptom return
Do not return to play on the same day as any new head impact
Allow more time for athletes with a high initial symptom burden [r7]

exercises.name: Full-contact practice
exercises.dosage: One or two sessions, then full team training, with symptom check after each
exercises.cues: Report any headache, dizziness or fogginess straight away

exercises.name: Return to match play
exercises.dosage: Progressive minutes, building to full matches over 1–2 weeks
exercises.cues: Coach and clinician monitor and watch for post-match symptoms

exercises.name: Neck strength and landing-tackle technique
exercises.dosage: Strength work 2–3 times a week; technique drills in training
exercises.cues: Good tackle technique and neck control are proposed protective factors [r12]

progressionCriteria: No symptoms with full-contact training, confirmed at 24 hours
Clinical and cognitive status normal or at baseline

criteria: Free of concussion symptoms at rest and with graded exertion (a common clinical convention)
Back to full school or work, or full study load, first [r5,r7]
Normal neurological examination, balance, cervical and vestibular-oculomotor screens (or back to baseline if tested)
Exercise tolerance normal, for example a normal result on a symptom-limited treadmill test where one was used [r21,r19]
Staged return completed with no symptom return after any step, with at least 24 hours at each step (clinical convention)
Medical clearance after full-contact practice, with agreement from the athlete and a plan for monitoring
tests: SCAT6 or Child SCAT6 and SCOAT6 for follow-up; the SCAT6 has limited utility as a return-to-play tool beyond 7 days, so it is not used alone [r16]
Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test or another graded exercise test [r19]
Vestibular and oculomotor screen and cervical examination [r18]
Symptom checks 24 hours after each step of the staged return
Medical clinical review before full-contact training

prognosis: Most athletes recover within weeks. A meta-analysis of 278 studies found a mean time to symptom-free of 14.0 days, with an RTS mean of 19.8 days and high heterogeneity [r7]. A minority have persisting symptoms: in 3063 children and adolescents, about one-third (31.0% of those followed) still had persistent post-concussion symptoms at 28 days [r11]. Factors linked to a worse course include a higher initial symptom burden, migraine, premorbid mental health problems, prior concussion with long recovery, continuing to play and delayed care [r7,r11]. For later life, a systematic review found no increased risk of mental health or neurological disease in former amateur athletes, with some signals in former professionals that need confirmation [r15].
prevention: Wear a properly fitted mouthguard in collision sports: protective effect IRR 0.74 (95% CI 0.64–0.89) [r12].

Support rule changes that reduce high-contact play: disallowing body checking in youth ice hockey was associated with a 58% lower concussion rate, and limiting contact in American football practice with a 64% lower practice rate [r12].
Use neuromuscular training warm-up programmes in rugby, where some evidence supports up to 60% lower concussion rates [r12].
Teach and enforce safe tackle technique and good neck control. Neck strength and technique are plausible but unproven modifiable factors, and the review called for more research [r12].
Recognise and remove from play any athlete with suspected concussion. Continued play and delayed care are associated with longer recovery [r7].
Teach athletes, coaches and parents the recognition tools and red flags (CRT6) so that injuries are reported [r5].
clinicalPearls: Lead with red flags. Any worsening headache, repeated vomiting, drowsiness, seizure or focal sign changes the pathway to emergency care before any concussion advice [r1].
Loss of consciousness is not required and its absence is not reassuring. Most concussions occur without it, and the diagnosis is clinical [r4].
Do not rely on imaging to rule concussion in or out. Imaging excludes bleeding and fracture; concussion is a functional injury with normal CT and MRI [r4,r1].
Avoid long strict rest. A 5-day strict rest group fared no better and had more symptoms than usual care, and early subsymptom aerobic exercise sped recovery in adolescents [r8,r21].
Always screen the neck, vestibular and oculomotor systems. If dizziness, neck pain or headache last beyond 10 days, begin cervicovestibular rehabilitation [r20].
The SCAT6 is for the first 72 hours to 7 days. Beyond that it has limited value as a clearance tool, so base return-to-sport decisions on a full clinical assessment and a staged return [r16].

captions.text: Two players run at each other during a contact game.
They collide at head and shoulder height at speed.
The head is struck and accelerates backwards, and the neck lets it rotate.
The player may stay on their feet and may not lose consciousness.
Headache, dizziness or fogginess follow. The player should leave the field and be assessed.
Zooming into the head, in a side-on section.

actions.text: Brain lags then strikes the skull
No bleeding or fracture: CT is normal

captions.text: The brain sits in cerebrospinal fluid inside the skull.
A blow to the forehead accelerates the head backwards.
The brain lags, then strikes the skull under the impact (coup).
It rebounds against the opposite pole (contrecoup).
Rotation strains the white matter, including the corpus callosum and brainstem.
There is no bleed or fracture. CT and MRI are normally normal, so diagnosis is clinical.
The injury is functional: a cascade of cell signalling and energy changes.
Healthy neurons: axons carry signals, with ions held in balance across the membrane.
Impact: the brain tissue is deformed by the forces.
Ions flood across the membrane and glutamate is released.
The cell pumps hard to restore balance, so energy demand rises: a period of metabolic crisis.
Balance returns over days to weeks, and most people recover. The timing varies.
